utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, good afternoon everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honour, to my learned friends from the Defence and to everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Matthias Neuner for the Prosecution assisted by Alma Imamovic-Ivanov or case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to the colleagues from the Office of the Prosecutor, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for the Defence of General Rasim Delic with legal assistant Lana Deljkic and our intern Tineke Baird.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, I believe this is your next witness. We can swear him in. Would you please make the declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seats, sir. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loncaric, as you know I will examining you on behalf of the Defence of General Delic. Since we speak the same language and since everything we say is interpreted, I will kindly ask you to speak as slowly as possible and to leave a short break after my question, so that we do not overlap. It is very important that everything that we say is entered into the transcript. Do you understand? Sir, will you state for the transcript your full name?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: My name is Alija Loncaric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of February, 1953, Pridvorica municipality of Gacko, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please come closer to the microphone so that we can hear you better. Thank you very much. Which schools have you finished?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I've completed the school for economics.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were you doing before the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I worked in the motor company Famos Sarajevo as a dispatcher.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, did -- had you had any sort of military education?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No, none.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of any political party before the war in Sarajevo -- Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what is the acronym under which this party is known?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of an organisation called Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain what sort of an organisation that is.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The Patriotic League is an organisation which gathered individuals and groups that were getting ready for defending themselves against the aggressors from the Republic of Serbian Montenegro. The organisation came into being within the Party for Democratic Action which, for the month of July was called the Crisis Staff and in the month of July, it was styled the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the month of July. Can you tell which year that was?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you a member of the Patriotic League or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of significance, if any, the Patriotic League had during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The Patriotic League had a great significance and influence in -- during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina because it was from the ranks of the Patriotic League that many individuals held important position, Sefer Halilovic was Chief of Staff, Kalisovic [phoen] was the head of the education administration, Mustafa --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Was the corps commander and later on he was on the head of the security administration Fikret Bilajac was in the ministry, the deputy of defence minister, Munib Mesic was a member of the Patriotic League, then the chief of the operations centre --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The interpreter is signaling to us that the -- not all the names were reflected in the transcript. Can we take this slowly please. You mentioned Sefer Halilovic as the Chief of Staff and that was entered in the transcript. Can you now please repeat but slowly and if you could come closer to the microphones, the names you referred one by one?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Kemo Karisik, chief of the administration for education.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please spell it out?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: K-E-M-O K-A-R-I-S-I-K.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, who was next?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Hajrulohovic, aka Talijan, commander of the 1st Corps later to become the chief of the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Munib Bisic, deputy defence minister. Suljo Zicrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you spell that name out, please.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: S-U-L-J-O Z-I-C-R-O-V-I-C, he was the chief of the operations centre of the staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Something else was entered into the transcript other than what you said. Can you repeat the last name?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Zicro Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now spell it out, please?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Z-I-C-R-O S-U-L-J-E-V-I-C.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was his function?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The chief of the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said he was the chief of what?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now briefly explain your career in the service during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, I was in the operations centre with Sefer Halilovic and the others who were members of the Patriotic League. When Sefer Halilovic was appointed the Chief of Staff, I became the head of office of his staff. And I held that position until early October of 1992. Next, I went to the logistics administration of the General Staff where I discharged my duties until August 1993. At that point, Sulejman Vranj became the chief of the administration, and I was transferred from logistics to the personnel administration, to the position of the chief of the section for education, decorations and citations, which was later to become the department for education, decorations and citations. In that department, I remained performing my duties until my retirement in 2000, and I retired with the rank of brigadier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come to know an individual by the name of Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us when and where you met that individual?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I met him in the earlier days in the month of April 1992 when the war broke out. We were working in the operations centre together. When I became Sefer Halilovic's head of office, Sakib Mahmuljin became secretary in the office. I left that post with Sefer, I said in early October 1992, and Sakib Mahmuljin continued working in Sefer Halilovic's office on that same post I referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown Exhibit 270, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before this document appears on the screen, let me ask you this: After you left Sefer Halilovic's office, did you maintain your contacts with Sakib Mahmuljin?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 270, for the record, this is the document of the staff of the Supreme Command dated the 15th of June, 1993, and the document is titled order.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we turn to the bottom part of the page, please. Thank you. So that we can see the end of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is a rather short document. Can you please read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I have read the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you knew Sakib Mahmuljin and that he had contacts with him. According to what you know, was Sakib Mahmuljin the head of office of the General Rasim Delic at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Sakib Mahmuljin was never his head of office. I'm familiar with this order, and the initials RK/DK mean that Rasim Mekic was the author of the document. As Sefer's cabinet underwent attrition because there was a new appointment for the commander, Sefer Halilovic could no longer afford to have a head of office and this order states that Sakib Mahmuljin should be transferred to become the head of office of General Rasim Delic. However, this order was never implemented. Murat Softic became Mr. Delic' head of office.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever come to know what the background of this order was and why it was not implemented?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Sakib Mahmuljin and, on one occasion, he told me that he wouldn't have dealings with Delic because he had his family outside of Sarajevo in the Zenica area and that he would rather be with his family, and that because of that, he went to see Mr. Izetbegovic relayed to him his request, and his request was granted by Mr. Izetbegovic. Thus, Sakib Mahmuljin went out to the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Izetbegovic, can you tell us what his function was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was the president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document can be removed now.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: What influence, if anything, did the fact that you should become the head of office of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, and I'm referring to Mr. Halilovic, have the fact that you didn't have any military experience, what bearing did it half?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the town council of the SDA party in Sarajevo and I was a member of the Patriotic League. I was together with Sefer Halilovic as of November 1991, and I knew him well. I was also on very good terms of the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, as well as with other members of the party. It was for that reason that I was trusted by Sefer Halilovic and was able to take up the position, because that was what mattered the most in those days, trust.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were on good terms with President Izetbegovic. How did you come to meet President Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I knew President Izetbegovic from the time when the SDA party had its electoral campaign and we attended some meetings, gatherings together. We met there, and this went on like that until the party won in the election. Afterwards, I had opportunity to frequently see President Izetbegovic in an office that was on the premises of the party offices. This was an office that we had as the Patriotic League and Mr. Izetbegovic used to come there, and we would inform him on the events and what it was that we were preparing so that we knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For a while, you worked in the cabinet or in the office of Sefer Halilovic. What was your view of the organisation of the army, the level of organisation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as perceived from where you were at the time, in the office of Sefer Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The degree of organisation of the army was very bad, low. What it meant was that there were individual groups of individuals that created units that later turned into brigades. There were daily shellings and sniper fire. There was no water or electricity, no foodstuffs. The army could not be in the barracks. They stayed -- the troop, they stayed at home, so we didn't have any materiel or technical resources. What we did have, what armaments we did have were on the front lines and when people were relieved on the front lines they would take their weapons home with them so that the organisation of the army was very poor at this time, if any. It was practically non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned at one point that these were groups that sort of grass root the groups that organised themselves and then later became brigades. What I would like to ask you is this: Before -- what was established first in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Brigades or corps?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Brigades were established first and then the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to observe how this affected the functioning of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the later days, in latter days, if any, because you were in logistics of the Main Staff at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: It functioned very poorly. And for several reasons. There were groups, units that were formed and then they turned into brigades. They selected commanders from among their own ranks. There were some that were very unethical, there were criminals among them and then you had, at one point in time you had the corps that were organised, and there were commanders who were from the former army, and this -- and this and when on up to the end of the war between those two categories. So you had on the one hand these self-organised elements and on the other hand you had educated men who were up to the level of the General Staff. The animosity between them went on throughout the war. There was disrespect, or, rather, at grass roots in the units there was no proper respect for the commands or the Main Staff, main command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are discussing 1992/1993. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992 and 1993, according to your knowledge, what was the influence of the Main Staff on personnel selection outside of Sarajevo, if there was any influence?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: There was none, and it was impossible because we lived in Sarajevo, we were surrounded. You couldn't leave the city. There was no communication; that's one. Two, the units had already been established before the Main Staff. They already existed. They appointed commanders from amongst themselves or these were local war lords, sometimes party leaders, and even some religious leaders so that there was no opportunity or possibility to command and control these units from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the period when General Delic became the chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when this was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: It was in the beginning of -- of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the situation in the Main Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I knew the situation in the Main Staff throughout the war. I was a member of the party, I was also in the town board of the party. I was in the staff -- there were men from the Patriotic League who were appointed to various duties throughout the staff so that I was well-informed throughout this period.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were -- you were employed or you worked at the Main Staff throughout 1993, you told us this, in logistics until August and ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last portion of his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you about -- in my previous question I asked you whether you worked at the Main Staff throughout 1993 up until August 1993, but your reply was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I was in the Main Staff in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1994 [as interpreted] in the logistics administration or personnel administration, but this was all within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, but this did not enter the transcript, Mr. Loncaric. Would you please just slow down a bit, because it is impossible to record everything you say, because you're speaking too fast, Mr. Loncaric. My last question was, what knowledge, if any, you had about the reception that General Delic received when he came to the Main Staff by the other members of the Main Staff. So could you please answer that question now.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delic was not well received by most members of the Main Staff, especially those members who were members of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Why was this so? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The men from the Patriotic League were all unified, and they worked at the Main Staff. They were -- they worked as one. Mr. Delic, when he was appointed for the army commander, we did not know much about him. We didn't know anything about him. And then there were rumours that he had arrived late, that he had been captured by the Green Berets so there were different rumours and we expected that the commander would be someone from the ranks of the Patriotic League. Since this did not happen, we did not accept him gladly. On the other hand, we also had information that Stjepan Siber proposed Mr. Delic for this position, and this came from the Territorial Defence. And there was always a clash between the Patriotic League and the Territorial Defence about who it was that really organised the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what nationality was Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Stjepan Siber was a Croat, I think that he declared to be a Bosnia-Herzegovina Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we now move to closed session and I would like the witness to see document D941 -- or, rather, can we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us that in August 1993 you started working in the personnel administration. From that position you held in the personnel administration, were you in a position to see how the command and control system worked, given the different relations within the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The command and control system could not function at all. If you have two opposed camps, then that makes it quite impossible for an entity to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us an illustration of what you mean and what you base your inference on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I will explain this to you by relay to go you one detail. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I will take the following example. When Mr. Delic signed the order whereby Asim Dzambasovic should be appointed to the operations centre and Zicro Suljevic should retire. However, the order was never implemented, because Zicro Suljevic went to see Mr. Izetbegovic and requested that he not be retired but that he be kept on the position he held. He enjoyed the support of others who were on good terms with Mr. Izetbegovic so that Mr. Dzambasovic showed up for his new duty but never took it up and never did that job. Subsequently, pursuant to an order Dzambasovic was assigned to the forward command post at Kakanj. In other words, the duty to which he was assigned by Delic, he never took up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And was he assigned to any other duty within the operations centre; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall. Dzambasovic was later on appointed as deputy, but again Mr. Suljevic and others who were working in the operations centre refused to take him on for the well-known reasons for the views that members of the Patriotic League held with regard to the individuals who came at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned other individuals whose appointments were discussed, namely Mustafa Polutak and you just mentioned Asim Dzambasovic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I also mentioned the order that was not implemented which had to do with the appointment of Mahmuljin Sakib as chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I'm inquiring now about the two individuals we were just discussing in this context. Mustafa Polutak and Asim Dzambasovic. Who were these individuals before the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: They were members of the JNA and had undergone military training, precisely for these jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to deal with a different topic. But before that, let me ask you this: What was your understanding of the situation as to why these two individuals were not accepted by members of the Main Staff, including Zicro Suljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: They were not accepted precisely because it was Mr. Delic who had ordered their appointment. At that time people did not have any respect for him, including myself. We had respect and we will the support of President Izetbegovic and that is why we were able to insist this those views of ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Delic do before the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the JNA. He was an officer of the JNA and the information we had said that he was one of the best schooled and trained officers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will now move to a different topic. You told us that by August 1993 up until the end of the war, you worked in the personnel administration of the staff of the Supreme Command. Who headed the administration at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: We're discussing the period through to the month of June until Delic's appointment. The administration for personnel and another administration were one, and Avdo Kajavic [phoen] headed that administration. When Mr. Delic took up his position as commander, the two administration again split into two --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to pause there. Can you please repeat the name of the individual who headed that administration?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Avdo Kajavic was the head of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you're saying, sir, that administration for personnel and another administration were one. What was the other administration. This is how your transcribed on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The administration for ORMB, organisation and mobilisation. ORMB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We need to understand from the witness, and you can ask him that question, what were really the dividing lines between those who were recruited from the old army and through the Territorial Defence, on the one hand, and then the Patriotic League on the on the other hand. Was it because of politics of the old army's communist background or was it military training or was it understanding of how Bosnia should are saved or where did the dividing lines go really. Did the members of the Patriotic League question the military ability and strength of the old members or ... What were the dividing lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the problem was not to be a member of the Patriotic League and come from the former army. If they -- if they joined the defence of the country on time. I mentioned Kajavic Avdo, for instance; Zicro Suljevic, Rifat Bilajac, Kemo Karisik, Mustafa Hajrulohovic, Talijan, Vahid Karavelic, and I can name 100 people or so, but all these men came back before the war started. In other words, the problem was not in communist or any other ideology the only problem was the moment they realized they should join the defence of the country. All these other men, officers of the former army, came to Bosnia when there was nowhere else they could go when the barracks in Sarajevo were disbanded and they could not join the other side, because they weren't accepted there. So in the situation in Sarajevo was such that even in May, there were people leaving the barracks, but between April and May, two or three months elapsed; April was already a wartime month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, it was basically a question of loyalty. Those who stood up for the country at once they were within the sympathy of the Patriotic League, and those who hesitated and only joined later on were looked down upon. Is that how we should understand this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your understanding is correct, except in the first part of what you said, Your Honour. There were members of the Yugoslav People's Army who joined the Patriotic League as early as -- in July 1991. One such person is Sulejman Vranj this mean there is were still seven or eight months before the war would break out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But this person that you mentioned, he would be respected, would he not, for having stood up quickly and -- so even if he came from the old army he would be enjoying the respect of the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, all those who joined up earlier, there were hundreds of those.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before the question was asked by the Honourable Judge, we were discussing the administration itself. You mentioned that it was split into two and you mentioned that of Avdo Kajavic had been before the split happened that he was the head of the entire administration. Now what happened when General Delic was appointed to the Main Staff, if anything with this administration?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The administration or MOB, organisation, mobilisation, and personnel was split and two new administrations were created so there was the administration for organisation mobilisation with Avdo Kajavic as the chief and the personnel administration was the new administration and at its head was now Sulejman Vranj.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like the witness to be shown Exhibit 1273 [as interpreted]. Your Honour, my assistant is signalling, I don't know if I made an error, but the number of the exhibit is 1283. We have a rather poor copy. We have a clear copy, hard copy, and perhaps we can have the assistance of the usher to show this copy to our colleagues from the Prosecution and then present it to the witness. Thank you. For the record, let me say that this is a document from the Main Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The personnel and legal administration, the document is dated 28 August 1995, and entitled opinion on engagement of foreign citizens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, just before you go -- are you sure this is an exhibit already?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document was a bar table document, a bar table exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll down the document a bit, so that we can see the signature. And you will be given sufficient time to take a thorough look at this document, Witness. Can we just see the signature on the document? Please scroll it down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncaric, do you recognise this signature?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: It was signed by Sulejman Vranj. He was my boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to quote a small portion of this document to you, the second paragraph where it is stated: "Therefore, foreign citizens can be engaged as members of the RBiH army provided that there is no founded suspicion that they participated or assisted in the aggression against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that they first make a written statement that they voluntarily wish to join the BH army. "Before engagement of each non-citizen of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is necessary to make security checks and try to find the actual reasons for their voluntary joining the BH army." Could you please, if you can, comment on this document? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do and the document is accurate. In fact, that is the way things have to be done the way it is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by saying the document is accurate? The administration you worked for, did it write such instructions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did write instructions, including this one, which is addressed to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this document an exception or did you send several such instructions to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were several instructions concerning the engagement of foreign citizens or aliens.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours can this document be assigned an exhibit number? Oh, I apologise, it is already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you several more questions before the break. You said that you worked in the personnel administration as of August 1993. In what way was the personnel administration organised?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The personal unit administration comprised two departments and one independent section.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which departments were those?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The first one was the department for personnel affairs; the second department was the one I worked for, for education, decorations and citations; and the third independent section was the section of legal affairs, and that's the section which authored this document. The person is Sakib Ibrahimovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for the additional explanation in relation to this document; namely, Exhibit 1283. Can you now describe the scope of work of your department; that is to say, the department for education, decorations and citations. I will, however, appeal to you again to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The department for education, decorations and citations that I was the head of only maintained records when it came to education. We did not have scores. We had the wartime officer's school in Zenica, but the staff there was within the purview of the education administration. Our job was only to maintain records. When it came to decorations and citations, we received from the corps various proposals for decorations, citations and incentives, which would be processed by my department, or, rather, by me personally, and at the end of this procedure, once decisions were made on the awarding of citations and incentives, I took the documents to the commander for his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the awarding of incentives and citations. Was this in any way regulated?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were the rules on awarding citations and incentives. The term used in the department, the decorations themselves, they were within the purview of the Presidency, which was entitled to award these.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain these matters to us more closely, since we are not privy to them. Is there a difference between decorations, citations and incentives? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can and I will. Decorations were of the highest rank.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is there a difference or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: There is an difference between decorations, citations and incentives. These are three categories of awards.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us where the difference lies now?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The decorations are the highest awards and were awarded by the Presidency. Citations and incentives lay within the purview of the commander. Decorations were awards of higher significance than incentives.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, interpreter's correction, citations were of a higher rank than incentives --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell what you say incentives are?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The golden lily, the green coat of arms, the lily of thankfulness, and the pluck of the armed forces as it was called, I believe, and the incentives were to be away, absent on -- as on awarded leave, honourable mention, stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you tell us now what sort of procedure applied for awarding citations and incentives?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Citations and incentives were normally awarded on the days that were the anniversaries of the corps, proposals would be sent to the corps, the corps would then process them, and then send them back to the staff, or, rather, to the personnel administration and to my department within that administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to stop here. I believe it is a time for a break and I will moving to a document that might take more than two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll use part of the remaining time just to get a little clarification. Sir, did there come a time when members or former members of the Patriotic League respected Rasim Delic and other former members of the JNA, and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the members of the Patriotic League did not accept Rasim Delic or respect him as they did not other members of the Main Staff who were former JNA officers and who I have to repeat, joined the defence effort at a later stage. Sakib Mahmuljin joined this effort in the month of April, and he was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understood that. Hence my question. Maybe my question was not properly accepted. I accept that that was the position. My question is as time went on, did relations improve between these two cliques such that there was mutual respect between former members of the of the Patriotic League and former members of the JNA and the TO. Did peace ever come about or did it stay like this until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Peace did come about, but to a lesser extent and only from some individuals. The relations remained as they were throughout the war and to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At about what time did this apparent peace come about? And -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Peace, if we can call it peace, what I mean is the fact that some former members of the JNA were accepted came about at the end of the war, after the war. When the war was over, some rapprochement could be noticed but it was again on individual basis. Some individuals were accepted, not all of them and this remains true to this day. Such are still the relations between us, members of the Patriotic League and the former JNA officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a personal question, and I don't meant to embarrass you, but did there come a time when you personally respected General Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did that come about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At some point after the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we go, what made you change your mind? If you don't want to share it, you can refuse to tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. At the point in time when he took up his duties, I didn't know anything about him. I knew that he was from the former JNA and that was the extent of it. However when the war was over there was more time to reflect on certain matters and more time to socialize with certain persons, and I had occasion to see that this was a good, honest man, who was very knowledgeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your candidure. We will take a break and come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be shown Exhibit 111. For the record, this is a proposal from the 3rd Corps command, for condemnations and incentives dated 10 November 1995, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would you please take a good look at page 1. We can see the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the top of both version, please. Perhaps you can scroll up the Bosnian version as well. Yes, that's how it should be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you just tell us, are there any indications that this is an encrypted document on this first page?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I can't find any of that. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see page 6 of the Bosnian and page 7 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document bear a signature?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we just scroll down the English version, although you can also see it from the Bosnian version. Thank you. And now can we see page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at this page. Let me just ask you, is this a document that resembles an official document, as far as you know, what these documents should look like?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No, because I see that there were some interventions. Something was handwritten on it and revised.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see anything here that you can comment on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see -- I think this is a draft version because I see names that are indicated there and then crossed out, scratched.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive documents of this type with notes like this in your administration?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No, we did not. A document had to be a clean version of a document without any changes to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can remove the document now. Thank you. You mentioned before the break that you were in the personnel administration, or, rather, in the department where you were working, that you received proposals for citations and incentives from corps commands. Can you describe briefly the role of the corps in this procedure, in the procedure of awarding citations and incentives, on the one hand, so what was the role of the corps in that; and on the other hand, the role of the personnel administration. Would you start with the corps please, step by step. And please take your time.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The corpses received proposals from the units within those corps. When they received a document from a unit they processed it and then forward the processed document to the personnel administration, or, rather, to my department directly, which I would then receive. This would be a document with proposals for awards of citations and incentives and if those proposals were in agreement with the rules on awarding citations and incentives then I would process this and prepare orders, and such orders would then be taken by me to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the role or the duty of the corps in preparing these proposals and -- as opposed to that of the administration?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The corps had the responsibility to prepare the documents according to the rules, and once they've prepared them to forward them to us. And if they had done so, if they had prepared them in keeping with the rules, and I believe they did, I would receive such proposals, process them, I would usually not interfere with the documents. I wouldn't add anything or take anything away from them once those documents were prepared in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And whose responsibility was it to check whether a person met the criteria as provided for in the rules, whether this person may have had a criminal record or a criminal -- or whether there was a person who could be awarded a citation?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: This was the obligation of the corps. It was not up to us to check the individuals, every individual who was proposed, because we did not receive just individual names. We would receive thousands of proposals, thousands of names. So that this was the responsibility of the unit or the corps to check the background of any or all of these individuals who are proposed for citations. It was not our duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you said that you checked whether the proposals were in keeping with the rules. Could you just describe or explain to us what exactly this meant? What is it you had to verify. You receive a list and then what do you do?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Well, there was -- there were the rules where it was provided for every citation and incentive what the individual would have had to accomplish in order to be proposed for this citation or incentive. Then, we would check and see the reasons that were provided by the corps for awarding a certain citation for -- to a certain individual and if it was in keeping with the rules, we would leave it there. If not, we would remove it.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you now describe the procedure. You said that you would take the document to the appropriate person for signature. Can you tell us what the procedure -- the proper procedure was. You mentioned that you would take this to the commander. Who was authorised to sign these orders for citations and incentives, as well as all other documents that your department produced?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The -- the authorised person was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. This was -- was this as a principle or as a rule or was he always the one who would sign such documents?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't always the case because we were in a state of war and often the commander was not in Sarajevo. He would be away for negotiations or something like that, and if the commander was not there, then I would take it to my boss, who, however, often was also not there, and my boss was Vranj at this time, in which case I would put the first and last name and then put an SR before that, meaning signed for, and such orders I would then forward on. There were other documents, there were -- there was a huge number of documents, because if a corps numbered 30.000 men and if only one per cent of those men were proposed for these citations that would mean there would be 3.000 names. Sometimes there were cases where there were 300 cases, 300 proposals, and signatures that were needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Would you --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown, please, Exhibit 570. For the record, I will say that this a Supreme Command Staff document, dated 25th of July, 1994, entitled proposal for promotion into ranks and this is submitted to -- and then the addressee follows. Can we just see the first page of the document and then if we could scroll it down a bit, so we can see both versions -- the bottom of the documents in both versions and then I would request to be shown the last page of the document. Thank you. The last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is General Vranj's signature and the document was prepared by Rasim Mekic and then /Damir Kalmar.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please repeat the name for the RM?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Rasim, R-A-S-I-M; Mekic, M-E-K-I-C, and the second name is Damir, D-A-M-I-R; Kalmar, K-A-L-M-A-R.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that this document was signed by General Vranj. Does that mean that General Delic had the opportunity to see this document? What was the usual practice? Would General Delic have been in a situation to see documents like these?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: General Delic did not see this document. It was signed in his name, and this document was then forwarded to President Izetbegovic where it was signed and where a decree was produced.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a moment ago that you took these documents to General Delic for signing personally. Were you in a position to see what the number of documents that he had to sign was?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I also had occasion to see other officers from the administration who were in the waiting-room there and usually I was the one with the greatest number of documents and my documents were usually of an urgent nature because they were urgent, I took them personally to the commander, and I took them into the office, asked for him to sign it, as soon as he did I would take them back because once they were signed there was still work to be done. In order for this to be implemented, I had to order the lilies to be produced and then I had to prepare the plaques that were to be awarded. I had to prepare watches that were going to awarded. So it was not just about signing the documents. It was a lot of work and it always had to be completed within two to three days and if you were late, and you couldn't afford to be late because there would be a celebration of an anniversary of a corps or so on, so this was very urgent. This procedure had to be followed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to this later. Before that, I would like to show you another document and then we'll discuss, talk about the signing later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 989. This is an order to improve the implementation of incentives and dated 20 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read the first paragraph of this document, Witness? And first let me ask you, have you ever seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received this document. I know who authored it. It was prepared in the morale administration. And it was sent to all corps commands and administrations, so I did receive it. And mention is made here of an analysis and errors that were made in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you now please take a look at page 2 of the document, in both versions. Please see number -- under number 1, under: Order. If we can just scroll the document down a bit. Please read that portion. I'd like to ask you this: Mention is made here of morale departments within corps commands. Tell us, what was the role of morale departments and morale administrations in this process of proposing awards?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Well, they were the ones who prepared the proposals. They took part in the proposal -- in the preparation of the proposals and then they would -- the corps would send them to us, which means that the administration for morale took part in the preparation of these proposals for awarding commendations, citations and incentives.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying then - I just want to check if I understood you correctly - are you then saying that two administrations actually took part in this process of preparing the proposals for awards? Was it two administrations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, you understood that well. There were two administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which administrations?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Morale and personnel administrations.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we please have an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit number 1374.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncaric, I would like to show you several documents now. Let us first ascertain whether you were the author of these documents, and after I have shown you several of these documents I will ask you to comment upon all of them. I believe that is the most efficient way of going through these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can the witness now be shown Exhibit 79. Can we focus on the bottom of the document. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm the author of the document. As you can see, it says Alija Loncaric. SP is Senad Pezo and then the initials of the person who typed the document up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says army commander -- commander army General Rasim Delic, SR. Is that the situation you explained earlier on?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the absence of General Vranj or General Delic, I would produce a document and place the acronym SR, which meant for their behalf and then once the document was processed and sent to the corps it wasn't sent to General Delic but was filed. It remained in the files and to me it meant that it was processed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was that the ordinary practice?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the ordinary practice in the absence of both General Delic and General Vranj had to keep the matters moving and could not wait for them to come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the document. It says here: Silver shield, war commendation.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back to page 1, so Their Honours can follow.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: It says, War citation or commendation, silver shield and earlier on when were talking about citations you said that silver shield was one of them but that's not a decoration, is it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No it is not a decoration.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness I will now ask you to read for us what is written underneath, I higher award ...

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: War citation silver shield for the members -- for the following members of the BH army and their names are listed here.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the errors in the translation of these documents. These were documents included in or tendered into evidence by the Prosecution where, instead of a citation, the awards, actions dated as decorations, and I believe the witness has drawn your attention to the difference between the types of awards, and I would like the translation to be rectified accordingly by the Prosecutor. If that could be done by the OTP, and if they could also ensure that it is uploaded into the system again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before Mr. Neuner gets the floor, I would just point to something that struck my mind on page 2 of the English version, it would seem that General Delic's signature was put there with his own hand, and that is exactly contrary to what I understood to be the meaning of SR.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. General Rasim Delic did not sign the document. That's why we can't see his signature. Wherever he sings it, you can see his signature. In cases such as this one, I would place this acronym SR, which stands for in his own hand, and then I just file the document, and carry the procedure further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpretation says SR means in his own hand, or does it mean on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not on his behalf. Where it is written army general, it is normally placed in inverted comas and then beneath that you would have the word "za 4," written and then somebody would sign for him. Instead in this case, I only write SR next to his name which actually means signed by him in person, and I put this down and then carry the procedure forward on the basis of this because it's a matter of an urgency.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. The transcript does not reflect what he says. I see you don't understand this. At no point did the witness say that he was signing the document for the General. Rather, the SR in his own hand, meant I am signing this in person. This is what it has the meaning of. I could grasp by your reactions that something was wrong. I am really unable to follow the interpretation that is being done here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because we are getting confused, you know. In his own -- SR meaning in his own hand, meaning your own hand, not his own hand. But it is your hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let me explain. There is no signature here at all. Mine or Mr. Delic's or anybody else's, because the document is an urgent one, and General Delic is absent as well as General Vranj who can't therefore sign on his behalf. These are urgent matters because units have their anniversaries and the matter cannot wait. In such situations I would write next to his name SR which meant that it wasn't signed by either General Delic, me, or somebody else and the document as such is forwarded into the subsequent procedure. I don't know if have I been clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I still have a problem with it. I would like to know exactly what the letters, the two words SR mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two letters stand for in his own hand, which means that the meaning of these two initials is equivalent to him having signed the document in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's very weird, that you would write in "svojervcno," whilst there's no signature by General Delic. It's -- I don't understand. I still have a doubt.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: May I say something? This was the time of war and we were working under wartime circumstances in times of peace you can discuss and debate whether he signed this or not. These were times of war we have a urgent meeting of the 3rd Corps and if General Delic is supposed to be absent for the following ten days I have to resort to this measure and put down SR as if he signed it personally, take it upon my own responsibility in order for the matters to be resolved. I don't know if I've been clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, does this mean that when General Delic would be absent, there was nobody among his deputies, the people who were supposed to act when he was not there, nobody who would be authorised to sign a document in his stead. I don't understand, because you see that would mean it was always upon the responsibility of General Delic and that nobody would be authorised to replace him. Have you to explain this to me, in light of this -- the absence of a signature here on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is true that there is no signature, but because this document was a matter of urgency where the anniversary of the 3rd Corps had to be celebrated I would place the letters SR next to his name. This was less painful, because the document could be processed, and the anniversary could be celebrated than me doing nothing and nothing being done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can understand that, but the things I don't understand is there was nobody else who would have been authorised to sign instead of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Sulejman Vranj was authorised to sign the documents in the commander's absence. Now, if both of them were absent, I don't know if there was somebody else, a third individual, that the commander may have authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this mean that the General saw the document or not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: No, as I said, no, I would send the document to such, to the units concerned, and file a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... briefly lengthy discussion, and we will bring this translation back to CLSS. As I just mentioned CLSS is our professional translation service. I believe they have looked up the word S.R. and we will ask them to revisit the issue especially also with regard to the word decoration which was mentioned by this witness, so we are trying to get a revised version. What this version will be or will look like, this is up for CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Neuner. Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was quite concerned to -- this is actually a matter of great concern to me, to hear that it is the CLSS who provides this sort of an interpretation of the document to the Prosecution. How can it be down to the CLSS to give their own interpretation of what SR stands for? It can only be provided by an expert who is knowledgeable about this, and as a result of this, we have such discussions in the courtroom. I believe that the English version should be corrected in order to reflect precisely what is stated in the original. SR and what these words stand for. I don't see why this should have to be translated at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why it is like that is because CLSS is the expert translator in this institution, Madam Vidovic. That's the only explanation I can give you and if they have mistranslated, so be it. And the witness has tried to explain to the best of his ability what it means. But that explains why CLSS translated that. They're given a document to translate. The document is got the letters SR, they translate those letters to mean: In my own hand. What can we do? Nothing. But the witness has told us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. While we still have this document on our screens -- or, rather, you don't have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If do you, can you please look at the introductory part of the document and tell us how it came to be?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The document was written on the occasion of the third anniversary of the inception of the 3rd Corps on the proposal of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I ask you about the relevance of this document. Quite looking aside from the issue of who signed the document, what is the probative value that the Chamber is going to pull out of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a document that was already admitted into evidence and was tendered by the Prosecution quite a while ago. I suppose the Prosecutor can tell you more about its relevance, but as far as I see it, it goes to show effective control in signing these documents, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well, for now. We'll probably get back to it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the point being made by the Defence is that this document was not signed by General Delic. He has no knowledge of it. There was no -- there was no effective control. That's the point being made by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was not how I understood His Honour Judge Harhoff's question. Perhaps it was again an issue of interpretation. Thank you. Can the witness now be shown Exhibit 827, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm advised this is a confidential document. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we open the window, please. Thank you. Yes, Madam Vidovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the witness now be shown, please, Exhibit 817. Could we just see the bottom or the end of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loncaric, have you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you take this document to be signed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I did all other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, speaking about the signing of these documents, you mentioned that if a document was several page document that you would submit it with the last page open where the signature should be placed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us how long did there signing take. Did the General inspect the documents one by one, or would he just sign them? How did this thing happen?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: General Delic did not have the opportunity either to read or to even look at the documents because there a lot of documents and they were all urgent. The commander signed them. I explained a moment ago how this was done. I brought hundreds of documents, not one or two or five. And had I left it for him to read them, it would take days. So he would just sign them.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, how did he -- did he look at the documents one by one or did you just prepare them and turn to the page where he is supposed to sign them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I explained a few moments ago he didn't look at them. I would put the documents on the table or if that wasn't possible on the floor and then I would hand him the documents one by one have him sign them and take it. Frequently he wouldn't even have time to ask me how I was doing. He would be taking a phone call and signing documents at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why General Delic did not pay attention to the contents of the documents?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: He didn't pay attention and he didn't even have to, because these were documents produced by the personnel department, by my department, and of course he had to trust this administration or trust me that we would prepare these documents in a proper fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, who would vouch for these documents that were signed by General Delic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: The administration for personnel, my department.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now remove this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like you to see several documents, and I will only ask you to look at them to make sure -- to find out if you are the author.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit 1134, please. Document 1134, please. For the record let me say this is a Main Staff document of 23rd December 1995. It is entitled order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, is this an exhibit or a document. The transcript shows both.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: We can see here the document. Tell us, please, have you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will show several documents of the same type, and then I will ask for them to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please just remember the date on this document, the 23rd December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see Exhibit 828, please. I will put the same question.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this document can now be removed. Let's take a look at Exhibit 829 and just pay attention to the date, the 23rd of December; you saw that. And now let's see 829.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you again what we are dealing with here is a war citation, not decoration. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you prepare this document?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say the date, 23rd December 1995. We saw several documents bearing the same date, 23rd December 1995, and for all these documents you confirmed that you were the author. Now, can you please try and remember and explain to us how these documents came to be, or how they were produced. Can you tell us how these documents were produced as far as the El Mujahedin Detachment, a detachment of foreigners is concerned. But, please, take your time, speak slowly so that it can enter into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. All three documents, I prepared. I was the author. These documents were made on the following basis: After the Dayton Accords, this unit was supposed to leave Bosnia and Herzegovina and we received information from Mr. Izetbegovic, the president, and Sulejman Vranj was in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, so we had information that they were not prepared to be disarmed easily and cease fighting. Our security services intercepted some of their conversations and we knew that they were not going to do this, that they would continue fighting, so that there was a political role here, political decision was made, and the political intervention, they spoke, the politician spoke with this unit and then Sulejman Vranj brought these documents, these proposals from me to prepare orders --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please pause here for a minute, because I see that the transcript does not reflect your words exactly. Did you say that the politicians talked with these units or did you say something else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I said that they talked with them and they negotiated with them, they tried to come to an agreement because we couldn't. And it was decided Mr. Izetbegovic called Mr. Sulejman Vranj to come and see him. He went and saw him, and he explained that these men were supposed to be awarded these citations, so that then they could leave the country. With all this, all of this should have been accompanied by reasons for these proposals. However, if we were to follow the rules -- however we just received the lists without any reasons, so I asked Sulejman Vranj how am I going to do this? There are no reasons. He said to me this was agreed with the president and he said there is how we should prepare it. And then I prepared these documents in contravention of the rules without any explanations as to what their contribution was. I prepared this document, or these documents, took them to Mr. Delic, he signed them and this was implemented, and I later found out that they -- that these men accepted this, and they left the country. Some of them remained, and the unit was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you something. How do you know that President Izetbegovic made this decision or that he talked with El Mujahid -- with them, you said. How do you know this? How did you come to learn about this?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA LONCARIC
utterances.text: I know that because there is what Mr. Vranj told me when he brought the three documents on the basis of which I was to produce orders. He personally told me that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, from whom did you learn all these details concerning the fact that they didn't want to go, they wanted to continue fighting. Who gave you all these details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was General Vranj who told me these details. He was the chief of the administration and he was one of the closest officers and party members to President Alija Izetbegovic and to the entire leadership of the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, he would have known that directly from the president. General Vranj would have known that directly from the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He would have learned that directly from President Izetbegovic, and he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Just before I ask Mr. Neuner to stand. One point or just one question. When they refused to stop fighting who were they going to be fighting now that there was no war any longer? There were no soldiers against whom they could fight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I don't know. That's the sort of explanation I heard from Mr. Vranj, who said that this was stated by President Izetbegovic. Who they wanted to continue their fighting against, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Loncaric. Mr. Neuner. Are you thinking you want a break before you started.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I could also go on for a few minutes, five minutes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Loncaric. I'm Matthias Neuner and I'm appearing here in behalf of the Prosecution.
